## Guides

## How often should you replace a hot tub filter?

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/how-often-to-replace-hot-tub-filter/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

Replacement intervals for hot tub filter cartridges from Hot Spring, Jacuzzi, Sundance, Unicel and Pleatco, and why there is no single number.

Most pleated spa cartridges are replaced somewhere between 12 months and 3 years, depending on the brand and how hard the tub is used. Jacuzzi says 12–24 months[10], Hot Spring says 2–3 years for standard cartridges[8]. Disposable inner filters (such as Sundance MicroClean inserts) are on a much shorter schedule of a few months[12].

## What the manufacturers say

SourceFilterReplace

Jacuzzi[10]Pleated cartridgesEvery 12–24 months, sooner if torn, flattened or heavily stained

Hot Spring[8]Polyester (“paper”) cartridgeEvery 2–3 years

Hot Spring[8]TRI-X cartridgeEvery 4–6 years

Hot Spring owner page[7]CartridgesEvery three years

Sundance 680 (2024 manual)[11]MicroClean Mini pleated filter / insert12 months / 4 months

Sundance 780 (2024 manual)[12]Small MicroClean disposable cartridgeEvery 3 months, or earlier

Note that Hot Spring’s own pages give slightly different figures (“every three years” on the owner maintenance page versus “2–3 years” on its filter article), so treat any number as a starting point, not a deadline.

## Why there is no fixed lifespan

Unicel and Pleatco both make the same point: a cartridge has no moving parts, so it doesn’t “fail” on a date. The media gradually plugs with body oils, soaps, chemicals and very fine particles[6][1]. They tie the end of a cartridge’s life to three things: shorter and shorter intervals between cleanings, low flow / high pressure, or physical failure such as torn media or a collapsed core[1].

## What makes a filter wear out faster

- More bathers and more frequent use (Hot Spring notes that more use means more frequent cleaning)[8].
- Unbalanced water chemistry[1].
- Scrubbing with a stiff brush[1], or unnecessary acid washing — Unicel calls acid washing “perhaps the biggest single factor leading to premature cartridge failure”[4].

## Stretch the life with two cartridges
Unicel, Pleatco and Jacuzzi all recommend alternating two sets of cartridges so one can be soaked and dried fully while the other is in use[6][1][10]. Find your replacement by OEM number on the homepage search, or browse Hot Spring, Jacuzzi and Sundance cartridges.

- Sundance Spas 680 Series Owner’s Manual (2024): https://cdn.spasoftwaresolutions.net/product_documents/sundance_spas/2024/6530-681L-English-Rev-A-13426123.pdf
- Sundance Spas 780 Series Owner’s Manual (2024): https://cdn.spasoftwaresolutions.net/product_documents/sundance_spas/2024/6530-607L-English-Rev-A-7862392.pdf

## How to clean a hot tub filter (step by step)

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/how-to-clean-a-hot-tub-filter/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

The cartridge cleaning procedure Unicel and Pleatco publish: hose rinse, degreasing soak, optional acid soak, and rinse — plus what to avoid.

Turn the spa off, remove the cartridge, hose it from the top down at about a 45° angle between every pleat, then soak it for at least an hour (overnight is better) in a filter cleaner, rinse thoroughly and reinstall. That is the procedure Unicel and Pleatco both publish[4][1].

## The full procedure

- Power off. Hot Spring and Jacuzzi both say to cut power before removing filters[9][10].

- Remove the cartridge following your spa maker’s instructions[4].

- Hose rinse. Use a straight-flow nozzle, work from the top down, hold it at about 45°, and focus between the pleats; rinse until all debris is gone[4][1].

- Degreasing soak. For spa cartridges, soak at least one hour (overnight is most effective) in a commercial filter cleaner, or 1 cup trisodium phosphate (TSP) per 5 gallons of water, or 1 cup dishwasher detergent per 5 gallons[4][1].

- Rinse again to remove oils and cleaner[4]. Jacuzzi warns that leftover residue can cause foaming once the jets run[10].

- Acid soak only if needed for mineral scale — see should you acid wash a spa filter?

- Reinstall and restart. Don’t overtighten the filter retainer[9].

## Things to avoid

- Stiff brushes on the media[1].
- Pressure washers or high-pressure nozzles that can tear fibers[10] (some Sundance manuals do call for a high-pressure hose nozzle on the outer pleated filter — follow your own manual[11]).
- Dishwashers and washing machines[10] — see dishwasher guide.
- Any cleaner on disposable inner inserts — Sundance says never to use filter cleaners on them[11].

## Using the spa while the filter soaks
Jacuzzi advises against running the spa with no filter installed; keep a second clean cartridge to swap in[10]. Hot Spring’s manual also says not to use the spa with the cartridge removed[9]. Look up a spare by part number on the homepage.

- Pleatco Catalog & Cross Reference Guide — filter care FAQ: https://cjp-manuals.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/Pleatco.pdf
- Pleatco FilterWash information sheet: https://lesl.a.bigcontent.io/v1/static/Pleatco-FilterWash-InfoSheet

## How often should you clean a hot tub filter?

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/how-often-to-clean-hot-tub-filter/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

Rinse and deep-clean schedules for spa filter cartridges according to Hot Spring, Jacuzzi, Sundance, Pleatco and Unicel.

A common baseline is a quick hose rinse weekly and a deep clean with filter cleaner every 4–6 weeks (Jacuzzi)[10]. Hot Spring recommends cleaning monthly[7][9], and Pleatco notes most spa makers recommend monthly, every two weeks with heavy use, and after parties[3].

## Schedules compared
SourceRinseDeep clean

Jacuzzi[10]Weekly (every 2–3 days with heavy use)Every 4–6 weeks (3–4 with heavy use; 6–8 with light use)

Hot Spring[8][9]MonthlySoak whenever you drain the tub

Pleatco[3]Monthly; every 2 weeks with heavy use; after heavy-use events

Sundance 680/780 (2024)[11][12]Clean the pleated filter monthly

Unicel[4]Set a routine based on how much the spa is used

## Can you clean too often?
Unicel notes cartridge filters use the debris they collect to improve filtration, so cleaning too often lowers efficiency while cleaning too rarely shortens cartridge life[4]. On systems with a pressure gauge (more common on pools), Unicel suggests cleaning when pressure rises 8 psi above the new-cartridge starting pressure[4].

## Signs you are overdue
Hot Spring warns a clogged filter can reduce jet performance, limit flow, and trip the high-limit thermostat[9]; Jacuzzi lists cloudy water, musty odor and FLO errors[10]. See signs your filter is bad.

## How to find your spa filter size

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/how-to-find-your-spa-filter-size/

Find the right replacement cartridge by its part number or by measuring diameter, length and end-cap fittings.

First look for a part number printed on the end cap or label and search it here. If there is none, measure the diameter across the widest point, the overall length end to end, and note the top and bottom fittings (open hole size, thread, handle or closed cap), then match them on the size lookup. These are the same fields Unicel and Pleatco catalogs list for every cartridge[5][2].

## Step 1: look for a number
OEM, Unicel (e.g. C-xxxx) and Pleatco (e.g. Pxxx / PRBxx) numbers can all be looked up from the homepage search. Our cross-reference comes from the Unicel 2026 Replacement Guide and the Pleatco 2023 catalog[5][2]. If your spa is a Hot Spring, Caldera, Jacuzzi, Sundance, Bullfrog or Master Spas, you can also look up the part by model and year: Hot Spring, Caldera, Jacuzzi, Sundance, Bullfrog or Master Spas. Two cartridges of the same size can carry different square-foot ratings; here is why.

## Step 2: measure
MeasurementHowWhy it matters

DiameterAcross the widest point of the pleats / end capMust fit the filter well or housing

LengthEnd to end, including any handle or threaded nippleMust fit the housing height

Top fittingOpen hole (measure inside), handle, or closedAffects how it is held in place

Bottom fittingOpen hole size, or male/female thread sizeMust seal on the standpipe or the water bypasses the media

Catalog tables list diameter, length, top and bottom fittings and media area (sq ft) for each cartridge[5][2]. See an example with a to-scale diagram: Caldera C-4335.

## Square footage is not the deciding factor
Media area (sq ft) helps distinguish two cartridges with the same dimensions, but match size and fittings first. Our measuring guide covers this in more detail.

- Unicel 2026 Replacement Guide: https://www.unicelfilters.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/2026-Unicel-Replacement-Guide.pdf
- Pleatco 2023 Catalog (Pentair): https://www.pentair.com/content/dam/extranet/nam/pentair-pool/residential/catalogs/pleatco/Pleatco-Catalog-2023-PRINT-Master.pdf

## OEM vs Unicel vs Pleatco spa filters: what’s the difference?

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/oem-vs-unicel-vs-pleatco-spa-filters/

Why the same hot tub cartridge has an OEM number, a Unicel number and a Pleatco number, and how cross-references work.

Spa makers (OEMs such as Hot Spring, Jacuzzi or Sundance) assign their own part numbers; Unicel and Pleatco are aftermarket cartridge makers that publish cross-reference tables mapping those OEM numbers to their own replacements[5][2]. A cross-referenced replacement is listed as matching the original’s dimensions and fittings.

## How the numbers relate
Who makes itExample numbering

OEMSold by or for the spa makerBrand-specific (e.g. Caldera 74148)

UnicelUnicel (aftermarket)C-xxxx (e.g. C-4335)

PleatcoPleatco (aftermarket)Pxxx / PRBxx (e.g. PRB35-IN)

Example from our data: Caldera OEM 74148 ↔ Unicel C-4335 ↔ Pleatco PRB35-IN, cross-referenced in the Unicel 2026 guide and Pleatco 2023 catalog[5][2].

## What spa makers recommend
Spa makers generally recommend their own filters: Hot Spring says to replace with genuine Watkins filters[7], and Jacuzzi recommends filters designed for your specific spa model[10]. Check your spa’s warranty terms before switching.

## Things to verify before buying

- Diameter, length and both end fittings match.
- Special designs (e.g. Hot Spring TRI-X, or Sundance two-stage assemblies with disposable inserts[12]) may not have a direct aftermarket equivalent.
- We flag rows we could not confirm in two sources as unverified.
Browse by brand: Caldera, Hot Spring, Hot Spot, Jacuzzi, Sundance.

## Signs your hot tub filter is bad (and needs replacing)

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/signs-your-hot-tub-filter-is-bad/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

How to tell when a spa filter cartridge is worn out rather than just dirty, according to Unicel, Pleatco, Jacuzzi and Hot Spring.

Replace a cartridge when cleaning no longer restores it: the time between cleanings keeps getting shorter, flow stays low, or the media is torn or the core collapsed[1][6]. Jacuzzi adds persistent cloudiness despite balanced water, limp pleats that don’t spring back, lasting odor after cleaning, cracked end caps, and flow errors right after cleaning[10].

## Checklist
SignSource

Shorter cycles between cleaningsUnicel, Pleatco[6][1]

Low flow / high differential pressureUnicel, Pleatco[6][1]

Torn media or collapsed center coreUnicel, Pleatco[6][1]

Limp or flattened pleats; cracked end capsJacuzzi[10]

Cloudy water or odor that persists after cleaning and balancingJacuzzi[10]

FLO / low-flow errors right after cleaningJacuzzi[10]

Discolored or worn mediaHot Spring[8]

## Discoloration alone isn’t proof
Pleatco notes that “white does not indicate clean” and media can discolor over time, while faded end caps can come from chlorine and cyanuric acid — though it can also indicate an old cartridge[3].

## Why it matters
Hot Spring warns a clogged filter can trip the high-limit thermostat and shut the spa off[9]. CDC advises regular cartridge replacement per the manufacturer as part of controlling germs like Legionella in hot tubs[14]. Ready to replace? Search your part number.

- Jacuzzi — Hot Tub Filter Cleaning Made Easy: https://www.jacuzzi.com/en-us/Hot-Tub-Filter-Cleaning-Made-Easy.html
- Hot Spring Spas — How Do Hot Tub Filters Work?: https://www.hotspring.com/blog/how-do-hot-tub-filters-work

## Spa filter cleaner vs DIY soaks (TSP, dishwasher detergent, vinegar, bleach)

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/spa-filter-cleaner-vs-diy-soak/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

Which cleaning solutions cartridge makers actually approve for hot tub filters, and which to avoid.

Unicel and Pleatco approve three soaks: a commercial filter cleaner, 1 cup TSP per 5 gallons, or 1 cup dishwasher detergent per 5 gallons[4][1]. Jacuzzi prefers commercial non-foaming cleaners, allows a 1:3 white vinegar solution for light mineral scale, and says to avoid chlorine bleach, harsh degreasers, bathroom cleaners and abrasive powders[10].

## Comparison
OptionWhat sources say

Commercial spa filter cleanerApproved by Unicel/Pleatco[4][1]; Jacuzzi’s preferred choice[10]; Hot Spring recommends a filter degreaser[9]

Trisodium phosphate (TSP)1 cup per 5 gallons, soak ≥1 hour[4][1]

Dishwasher detergent1 cup per 5 gallons[4][1]; Jacuzzi warns detergents can foam if not rinsed extremely well[10]

White vinegar1 part to 3 parts water for light mineral scale; weak on oils[10]

Chlorine bleachAvoid — can damage fibers[10]; Pleatco says bleaching agents can damage filtration fabric[3]

Muriatic acidOnly for confirmed mineral scale, after degreasing — see guide

## Special cases

- Biguanide (Baquacil) users: Unicel and Pleatco say the cartridge must be cleaned with Baqua Clean before any cartridge cleaner[4][1].
- Disposable inserts: Sundance says never use filter cleaners on its inner inserts[11].
- Tablets: Pleatco FilterWash is meant for a 25–30 minute soak and the solution should not be saved[3].
Always rinse thoroughly before reinstalling. Need a fresh cartridge instead? Find yours.

- Pleatco FilterWash information sheet: https://lesl.a.bigcontent.io/v1/static/Pleatco-FilterWash-InfoSheet

- Sundance Spas 680 Series Owner’s Manual (2024): https://cdn.spasoftwaresolutions.net/product_documents/sundance_spas/2024/6530-681L-English-Rev-A-13426123.pdf

## Should you acid wash a spa filter?

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/should-you-acid-wash-a-spa-filter/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

When muriatic acid soaking is appropriate for a hot tub cartridge, Unicel’s bubble test, and the safety rules.

Usually not. Unicel calls acid washing “perhaps the biggest single factor leading to premature cartridge failure” and says to acid wash only when required, and never without degreasing first[4]. If a drop of acid on clean, rinsed media bubbles, there’s mineral buildup and a mild soak of 1 part muriatic acid to 20 parts water is the published remedy[4].

## Unicel’s bubble test

- Degrease the cartridge thoroughly and rinse away all soap[4].
- Put a few drops of acid on a small area of media.
- Bubbling = calcium/mineral buildup → mild acid soak. No bubbling = no acid wash needed[4].

## The soak
1 part muriatic acid to 20 parts water until bubbling stops, then rinse[4][1]. Unicel warns that acid-soaking before removing all oils and cleaner causes a permanent flow restriction[4].

## Safety

- Wear rubber gloves and safety glasses; don’t add water to acid; never mix chlorine and acid[4].
- Jacuzzi says strong acids like muriatic acid should only be used by professionals and never as a first-step cleaner[10].

If the cartridge is old and scaled, a replacement may be the safer choice — search your part number.

### Sources
- Unicel — Maintenance & FAQ: https://www.unicelfilters.com/maintenance-and-faq/
- Pleatco Catalog & Cross Reference Guide — filter care FAQ: https://cjp-manuals.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/Pleatco.pdf
- Jacuzzi — Hot Tub Filter Cleaning Made Easy: https://www.jacuzzi.com/en-us/Hot-Tub-Filter-Cleaning-Made-Easy.html

## Can you put a hot tub filter in the dishwasher or use a pressure washer?

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/can-you-put-a-hot-tub-filter-in-the-dishwasher/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

What Jacuzzi, Pleatco and Sundance say about dishwashers, washing machines, pressure washers and stiff brushes on spa filter cartridges.

No to the dishwasher: Jacuzzi says dishwashers and washing machines aren’t recommended because high heat and aggressive spray can warp end caps and don’t clean deep between the pleats[10]. For rinsing, use a garden hose; Jacuzzi says to avoid pressure washers that can tear fibers[10].

## Quick answers
MethodVerdict

Dishwasher / washing machineNot recommended[10]

Pressure washerAvoid — can tear fibers or damage seams[10]

Garden hose, top-down at ~45°Recommended[4][1]

Stiff brushNever on the media[1]

Dishwasher detergent as a bucket soakAllowed by Unicel/Pleatco (1 cup per 5 gal)[4][1]

Note the difference: putting dishwasher detergent in a soaking bucket is a published option; running the cartridge through a dishwasher is not. Sundance’s 2024 680 manual specifies a high-pressure hose nozzle for its outer pleated filter but a low-pressure nozzle and no chemicals for the insert[11] — follow your own spa’s manual. Full steps in how to clean a hot tub filter.

## Best hot tub test strips and test kits: how to choose

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/best-hot-tub-test-strips/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

What test strips and kits actually measure, which readings matter for chlorine vs bromine tubs, and a short list of strips and DPD kits to consider.

Pick strips that read your sanitizer (free chlorine or bromine), plus pH, total alkalinity and calcium hardness. CDC says to use test strips to check disinfectant and pH[13], and Hot Spring’s own recommended ranges are free chlorine 1–5 ppm, pH 7.2–7.8, total alkalinity 40–120 ppm and calcium hardness 75–150 ppm[18].

## What you are testing for

ReadingRange given by sourceSource

Free chlorine1.0–5.0 ppm (Hot Spring owners) · at least 3 ppm (CDC hot tub rash page)[18][13]

Bromine4–8 ppm[13][14]

pH7.2–7.8 (Hot Spring, CDC Legionella toolkit) · 7.0–7.8 (CDC rash page)[18][14][13]

Total alkalinity40–120 ppm (Hot Spring)[18]

Calcium hardness75–150 ppm standard; 25–75 ppm with Hot Spring’s salt system[18]

The ranges differ a little between sources, which is normal: CDC’s numbers are public-pool baselines, while a spa maker’s numbers are tuned to its own equipment. Follow your owner’s manual if it gives different numbers.

## Strips vs liquid (DPD) kits

Strips are quick: you dip, wait and compare the colors to the chart, which Hot Spring describes as giving “a working range” for pH, alkalinity, hardness and chlorine[18]. Liquid reagent kits (the DPD kits below) take more steps and are usually chosen when you want finer readings. CDC’s chemical-safety page also notes that if a reading is off the top of the scale you may need dilution or higher-range strips[15].

## How to choose

- Match the sanitizer. A strip made for bromine reads bromine; a chlorine strip reads chlorine. The AquaChek “Red” and “Yellow” listings below make this split in their titles.

- Salt-system tubs need the right strip. Hot Spring warns that calcium tolerances are lower with its salt system, so use the strips made for your spa model[18].

- Check the date and keep the bottle closed. Strips are color chemistry; follow the package instructions for timing and storage.

- Test often. CDC’s toolkit tells public hot tub operators to test disinfectant and pH at least twice a day[14]; home owners usually test less often, but more frequent testing is better in heavy use. Check your own manual for its schedule.

## Why bother
CDC links hot tub rash to sitting in a poorly maintained tub and recommends checking disinfectant and pH with test strips[13]. Our pH and alkalinity guide covers what to do with the numbers.
Product lists below are picks, not rankings. We checked that each Amazon listing exists and what its title says; we have not lab-tested any product, and we do not publish prices or star ratings because they change. Match any product to your spa maker’s guidance, and keep the label directions as your final word.

### Sources
- Hot Spring — How do I choose the right spa chemicals for my hot tub?: https://www.hotspring.com/faq/how-do-i-choose-the-right-spa-chemicals-for-my-hot-tub
- CDC — Preventing Hot Tub Rash: https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-swimming/prevention/preventing-hot-tub-rash.html
- CDC — Controlling Legionella in Hot Tubs: https://www.cdc.gov/control-legionella/php/toolkit/hot-tub-module.html
- CDC — Pool Chemical Safety (applies to pools, hot tubs and spas): https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-swimming/toolkit/pool-chemical-safety.html

## How to balance hot tub pH and alkalinity (in the right order)

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/how-to-balance-hot-tub-ph-and-alkalinity/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

Total alkalinity first, then calcium, then pH: the order Hot Spring’s manual gives, target ranges, how to add chemicals, and pH/alkalinity products to consider.

Hot Spring’s 2026 owner’s manual says to adjust total alkalinity first (target 80 ppm), then calcium hardness (target 100 ppm), then pH (target 7.4–7.8), because out-of-balance alkalinity affects your ability to adjust pH and keeps sanitizer from working effectively[9].

## The order and the targets

StepTargetAcceptable range

1. Total alkalinity80 ppm40–120 ppm

2. Calcium hardness100 ppm (50 ppm with salt system)75–150 ppm (25–75 ppm with salt system)

3. pH7.4 (manual); 7.4–7.8 start-up instruction7.2–7.8

Figures are from Hot Spring’s Hot Spot owner’s manual[9] and its chemical FAQ[18]. CDC’s Legionella toolkit also lists pH 7.2–7.8[14]. Your own spa’s manual is the controlling document.

## How to add the chemicals

- Test first with a strip or kit (see test strip guide).

- Add through the filter compartment with the jets on high. Hot Spring says granulated pH increaser/decreaser and alkalinity increaser go directly into the filter compartment with the jet pump on high for at least ten minutes[9].

- Measure carefully and avoid splashing on hands, eyes or the shell surface[9].

- Retest, then adjust again in small steps rather than one big dose.

## Which product for which problem

- Alkalinity or pH too high: a pH/alkalinity decreaser (“down”). Hot Spring lists high total alkalinity/pH as a probable cause of scale and recommends pH/alkalinity down[19].

- Alkalinity or pH too low: alkalinity increaser or pH increaser (“up”). Hot Spring lists low total alkalinity and/or pH as a probable cause of staining when source water also has iron or copper[19].

- Calcium low: a calcium hardness increaser, mainly for soft fill water.

## Safety

- Read the label and safety data sheet and use protective equipment; CDC’s pool-chemical page says injuries happen when chemicals are mixed or protective equipment is not used[15].

- Never combine two chemicals in one container or pour them together; add one at a time. CDC says to store each product separately, in its original labeled container[15].

- Hot Spring’s manual says not to use chemicals other than those recommended by Watkins Wellness or its dealers[22]. If your tub is under warranty, ask your dealer before switching brands.

## Hot tub sanitizer: bromine vs chlorine vs mineral systems

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/best-hot-tub-sanitizer-bromine-chlorine-mineral/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

How the main hot tub sanitizers differ, what CDC and Hot Spring say about residual levels and stabilized chlorine, and a short list of tablets, floaters and granules.

CDC’s target residuals for hot tubs are free chlorine 3–10 ppm or bromine 4–8 ppm with pH 7.2–7.8[14]; Hot Spring’s owner range for chlorine is 1–5 ppm[18]. Whichever you choose, you need a test kit that reads it. One caution: CDC’s toolkit says cyanuric acid / stabilized chlorine products should not be used in hot tubs because they slow disinfection[14], while Hot Spring’s own manual uses sodium dichlor (a stabilized chlorine) for superchlorinating[9]; follow your spa maker.

## The three common approaches

SystemHow you use itWhat to know

BromineTablets in a floater or in-line feeder, with a sodium-bromide “bromine reserve” sometimes used to startCDC lists bromine 4–8 ppm for hot tubs[13][14]. Needs a strip or kit that reads bromine.

Chlorine (granules)Measured doses of granules, added through the filter compartmentHot Spring’s range is 1–5 ppm free chlorine[18]; CDC says 3–10 ppm[14]. Check the label for “stabilized/dichlor” (see the CDC note above).

Mineral / cartridge systemsA cartridge or floater that releases a sanitizer or mineral over weeksSome products pair with a conventional sanitizer, so read the label. Follow the product’s own instructions and still test the water; the listings below describe what each product says it is.

## Choosing

- Start from your owner’s manual. Hot Spring’s manual specifies adding chemicals through the filter compartment with the jets on high[9]; some spas ship with an in-line feeder instead.

- Floaters: a floating dispenser holds tablets sized for it, so check the tablet size on the listing. The two floaters below say they fit 1-inch tablets (440) or chlorine and bromine tablets (U.S. Pool Supply).

- Don’t switch sanitizers casually. Moving between bromine and chlorine is covered in your spa maker’s instructions; don’t guess.

- Hot water changes things. CDC notes that hot tubs sit in the temperature range favorable to Legionella (77–113°F) and make aerosols and speed up disinfectant decay[14], which is why a steady, measured residual matters more than any brand.

## Handling and storage
CDC says to store pool chemicals below 95°F, away from sun and moisture, in their original labeled containers, with each product stored separately and incompatible chemicals kept apart[15]. See our chemical safety guide.

## Hot tub shock: chlorine vs non-chlorine (and when to use it)

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/hot-tub-shock-chlorine-vs-non-chlorine/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

What “shocking” a hot tub means, what Hot Spring and CDC say about superchlorinating, and non-chlorine oxidizers to consider.

“Shock” is a higher-than-normal dose of oxidizer. Hot Spring’s manual superchlorinates new water with 1½ teaspoons of sodium dichlor per 250 gallons and lists MPS (non-chlorine shock) among the chemicals added through the filter compartment[9]. Hot Spring’s troubleshooting page repeatedly lists “shock spa with sanitizer” as a fix for water problems[19].

## Two kinds of shock

- Chlorine shock (such as dichlor granules) raises chlorine for a while. Hot Spring’s start-up routine uses it[9]. CDC’s toolkit footnote cautions against stabilized chlorine in hot tubs[14], so confirm what your spa maker recommends.

- Non-chlorine shock (MPS or similar oxidizer) is sold to oxidize contaminants without raising chlorine; Hot Spring’s manual includes “MPS” in the list of chemicals it tells owners to add to the filter compartment[9]. Several listings below describe themselves as non-chlorine.

## When to shock
Hot Spring’s troubleshooting list includes shocking when water is affected by dirty filters, excessive oils or organic matter, improper sanitizing or overused water[19]. It also advises letting free chlorine fall below 5 ppm before using the spa when the level is above 5 ppm[19], so always wait and re-test after shocking.

## How to do it safely

- Cover off, jets on high, chemicals into the filter compartment, ten minutes minimum[9].

- Measure the dose from the label for your water volume; don’t eyeball it.

- Follow the label for how long to wait before anyone gets back in, then re-test and wait until chlorine is back in range (Hot Spring says below 5 ppm[19]).

- Store leftover product dry, separate from other chemicals and sealed in its original container[15].

When the water won’t clear after shocking, see our foam, cloudy water and jet cleaner guide; a clogged cartridge is a common reason, so clean the filter too.

## Best hot tub filter cleaners: soaks, sprays and tools

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/best-hot-tub-filter-cleaners/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

Soak vs spray vs DIY, what Unicel and Pleatco say about degreasing, and a short list of spa filter cleaners and cleaning tools.

Unicel and Pleatco both say a spa cartridge needs a degreasing soak of at least one hour (overnight is best) in a commercial filter cleaner or a DIY alternative after a hose rinse[4][1]; a purpose-made cleaner saves the guesswork. Always rinse thoroughly afterward because leftover residue can cause foaming[10].

## Soak, spray or DIY?
MethodNotes

Concentrated soak (liquid or powder)Dilute per label, submerge the cartridge, rinse. Matches the one-hour minimum Unicel and Pleatco describe[4][1].

Spray-on cleanerSpray, wait per label, rinse. Convenient between full soaks; read the label for contact time.

DIY soakUnicel/Pleatco list TSP or dishwasher detergent in a bucket; see cleaner vs DIY.

## What to look for

- Made for cartridge filters — look for “filter cleaner” or “cartridge cleaner” on the label.

- Match your spa maker. Hot Spring names its own filter cleaners as the fix for dirty filters in its troubleshooting table[19], and its manual tells owners not to use cleaners other than those recommended by the maker or dealers[22]; check before using other brands on a warranty tub.

- Quantity: a soak needs enough solution to submerge the cartridge, so bottle size matters more than price per ounce.

- Don’t add an acid soak by habit. Unicel warns acid washing is a major cause of premature cartridge failure[4]; see our acid wash guide.

## Tools
The Filter Flosser listing describes itself as a cartridge filter cleaner for pools and hot tubs; Unicel and Pleatco tell you to use a straight-flow hose nozzle at about 45° and never a stiff brush on the media[4][1], and Jacuzzi warns against high-pressure tools[10], so judge any tool against those limits.

Full step-by-step: how to clean a hot tub filter. Need a spare to swap in while one soaks? Search your part number.

## Hot tub stain, scale and metal control: causes and products

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/hot-tub-stain-scale-and-metal-control/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

What causes scale and metal staining according to Hot Spring’s troubleshooting guide, how stain-and-scale products are used, and options to consider.

Hot Spring’s troubleshooting guide ties scale to total alkalinity and/or pH being too high and high calcium in the water, and staining to total alkalinity and/or pH being too low plus iron or copper in the source water; it recommends balancing the water and adding its Stain & Scale product to inhibit metals[19].

## Two different problems
ProblemProbable causes (Hot Spring)Fix (Hot Spring)

ScaleTotal alkalinity and/or pH too high; high calcium content in the waterLower alkalinity and pH; if scale must be removed, drain, scrub it off, clean the shell, refill; add a stain-and-scale product and rebalance[19]

Staining / discolorationTotal alkalinity and/or pH too low; high iron or copper in source waterRaise alkalinity/pH; use a stain-and-scale product to inhibit metals[19]

## How the products are used
Hot Spring’s manual lists “liquid stain and scale inhibitor” among the chemicals added directly into the filter compartment with the jet pump on high for ten minutes[9]. Metal-control products (such as the “metal gon” and “metal free” names below) are sold for the same fill-water problem; follow each label’s dose and timing.

## Prevent it first

- Keep alkalinity and pH in range; see the balancing guide and measure with good test strips.

- CDC’s Legionella toolkit notes sediment and biofilm are key factors and recommends scrubbing surfaces each time the tub is drained[14].

- If your fill water is hard or has metals, a hose-end pre-filter on the fill hose may help; search below because the right size depends on your hose.

- Scale on the cartridge is a separate issue: see acid washing.

## Hot tub foam, cloudy water and jet cleaners: what to try

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/hot-tub-foam-cloudy-water-and-jet-cleaners/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

Probable causes Hot Spring lists for cloudy water and other problems, when defoamers, clarifiers, enzymes and plumbing flushes are used, and a short list of products.

Start with the cause, not the bottle. Hot Spring lists dirty filters, excessive oils or organic matter, improper sanitizing, suspended particles and overused or old water among probable causes of water problems, and its fixes run from cleaning filters and shocking to draining, cleaning and refilling[19]. Defoamers, clarifiers and enzymes are add-ons after that.

## First checks

- Clean the filter. It is the first fix on Hot Spring’s list[19]; see how to clean a hot tub filter. Jacuzzi warns that leftover cleaner can foam once jets start[10].

- Test sanitizer and pH. Hot Spring pairs low pH or low sanitizer with several water problems[19].

- Shock if needed (see the shock guide).

- Consider the water’s age. CDC gives a formula for how often to replace hot tub water: (spa volume in gallons ÷ 3) ÷ average number of users per day, as days between changes[14]. A 400-gallon tub with 2 users a day works out to 400 ÷ 3 ÷ 2 ≈ 67 days.

## What each product type is for
TypeUse

DefoamerKnocks down surface foam. Hot Spring lists liquid defoamer among chemicals added to the filter compartment[9]. Foam usually returns if the cause (oils, residue, old water) stays.

ClarifierSold to help the filter catch fine particles; not a substitute for a clean cartridge.

EnzymeSold to break down oils and lotions; the listings below describe this.

Jet / plumbing cleaner or flushRun through the plumbing before a drain to loosen buildup. CDC’s toolkit recommends scrubbing surfaces and cleaning filters whenever the tub is drained[14].

## When to drain
Hot Spring’s last-resort fix for almost every problem is to drain, clean and refill[19]. If water is still cloudy after filter cleaning, shocking and balancing, plan a drain.

## Hot tub cover lifters and cover care: what to know before you buy

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/hot-tub-cover-lifters-and-cover-care/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

How cover lifters differ by clearance, Hot Spring’s cover cleaning and handling rules, wind and snow cautions, and cover lifter options.

Choose a lifter by the clearance behind your tub: Hot Spring’s own lifters need 24 inches (CoverCradle), 14 inches (Lift ’n Glide) or 7 inches (UpRite) behind the spa and 3 inches at the sides, and its manual says never to lift a cover by its skirting or lock straps[20][22]. Whatever you use, keep the cover locked when the tub isn’t in use[16].

## Pick a lifter by clearance
Hot Spring lifterBack clearanceSide

CoverCradle / CoverCradle II24 in3 in
Lift ’n Glide14 in3 in
UpRite (also a privacy screen when open)7 in3 in

[20] Hot Spring notes actual clearance varies by model and location, and that its lifters hide the cross bar inside the cover seam; not all lifters are built that way[20]. Third-party lifters like the two below are universal-style: check the listing’s dimensions against your cover and the space behind your tub. Hot Spring’s manual tells owners not to use lifting mechanisms other than those recommended by the maker or its dealers[22], so if you own a Hot Spring under warranty ask your dealer first.

## Cover care (from Hot Spring’s manuals)

- Clean monthly. Hose it, then use a very mild soap solution (1 teaspoon dish soap in 2 gallons of water for vinyl) with a soft brush and rinse so the soap film doesn’t dry on it[21][22].

- Underside: water only, then wipe dry[21].

- Vinyl only: Hot Spring’s Cover Shield conditioner is for vinyl covers and should not be used on polyester[21]. Other brands’ protectants: read the label for your cover material.

- Don’t drag the cover by the flaps or lock straps, walk or sit on it, put metal or heat-transferring objects or a plastic tarp over it[22].

- Snow: remove buildup to protect the foam core[22].

- Wind: Hot Spring says its cover and retractable systems aren’t recommended in winds above 25 mph (40 km/h), and extra cover-lock straps can be added where wind is a problem[22].

## Safety
CPSC’s tips: always use a locked safety cover when the spa is not in use, and keep young children away unless there is constant adult supervision[16]. CPSC also warns that a solar cover can let a child slip into the water while the cover appears to stay in place[17]; a solar blanket is not a safety cover.

## Hot tub steps and handrails: sizing and safe-entry checklist

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/hot-tub-steps-handrails-and-safe-entry/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

How to choose hot tub steps and a handrail by height and footprint, plus the CPSC safety tips that apply around any spa.

Measure first: the step must reach from the ground to the tub’s rim height without a big gap, and fit the space beside the tub. CPSC’s spa tips also apply: use a locked cover when not in use, keep water at 104°F or below, and avoid alcohol while soaking[16].

## Choosing steps (editorial advice)

- Measure rim height from the ground (or deck) to the top of the shell, and compare it with the step’s stated dimensions on the listing; the listings below describe themselves as three- or four-step units or a two-tier storage step.

- Footprint: the listing says 36 inches wide for the storage step. Check that your path to the tub isn’t blocked.

- Non-skid surface: the storage-step listing says non-skid; look for the same on any step you buy.

- Stable ground. Place steps on a flat, firm surface.

## Handrails
Handrails vary in how they attach: freestanding, clamp-on, or sliding under the cabinet. The Zelen listing says it adjusts from 39 to 60 inches and rotates 360°; confirm that it fits your spa’s cabinet and weight rating on the listing. Because attachment varies by spa, we also link a search so you can compare options.

## Safety (from CPSC)

- Always use a locked safety cover when the spa is not in use, and keep young children away unless there is constant adult supervision[16].

- Know where the pump cut-off switch is, check that drain covers are in place and not cracked or missing, and keep the water at 104°F or below[16].

- If a child is missing, look in the pool or spa first[17].

- Whatever steps or rails you add, keep the cover locked when the tub is not in use[16].

Also see cover lifters and cover care.

## Hot tub cleaning tools: skimmers, vacuums and scum absorbers

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/hot-tub-cleaning-tools-skimmers-and-vacuums/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

What hand skimmers, mini spa vacuums and scum absorbers are for, with CDC guidance on scrubbing and draining, and a short list of tools.

Tools handle what chemicals can’t: leaves, hair and debris, scum lines and the sediment on the floor. CDC’s toolkit says to scrub all surfaces each time the tub is drained[14], and Hot Spring says to wipe off scum with a clean rag and, if severe, drain and clean the spa[19].

## What each tool does
ToolGood for

Hand skimmerLeaves, bugs and floating debris; take it out before they sink and decay.

Mini spa vacuumSediment and grit on the seat and floor. Listings below range from manual to battery-powered or rechargeable.

Scum absorberA sponge that floats to soak up surface oils.

## Choosing

- Soft contact with the shell. Hot Spring’s quick start says household chemicals are harmful to the shell and a soft rag removes most dirt[21]; avoid abrasive pads or stiff brushes.

- Size. Compare the listing’s reach with the depth of your tub.

- Power. Manual vacs need no charging; battery or rechargeable ones need to be kept dry between uses.

- Electric safety: don’t use mains-powered tools in or beside the water.

## Routine

- Skim as needed; wipe the waterline with a clean rag[19].
- Vacuum before shocking so loosened debris reaches the filter.
- At each drain: scrub every surface[14] and clean the filter (how often?).

## Replacement hot tub headrests and pillows: how to get the right fit

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/replacement-hot-tub-headrests-and-pillows/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

Why spa pillows are model-specific, how to measure and identify yours, and search links for pillows and headrests by brand.

Spa pillows are model-specific: mounting style, size and shape differ by maker and often by model year, so we link brand-specific Amazon searches rather than a single product. Identify your spa’s make and model first, then match the pillow’s listing text against your old one.

## Identify what you have

- Find the make and model on the cabinet label, the manual or the control panel.

- Look at the old pillow: does it clip, suction-cup, or use a pin or insert? Measure width, height and thickness.

- Read the new listing’s model fitment and the part number if one is given; some listings name the spas they replace (for example, a pillow listing may name a specific brand and year range) — confirm the year range.

## Material and care

- Pillows sit in hot, chemical-laden water and will wear. Rinse them with fresh water and keep sanitizer in range[14].

- Hot Spring’s quick start says most household chemicals are harmful to the spa shell[21]; use mild products on pillows too and rinse well.

## New or generic?
A manufacturer part usually matches the clips exactly; generic replacements can be cheaper but you must verify dimensions and mounting. Our Hot Spring, Jacuzzi, Sundance and Caldera pages cover your filters; for pillows, start from your model name on the searches below.

## Hot tub chemical safety and storage: what CDC says

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/hot-tub-chemical-safety-and-storage/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

CDC’s pool-chemical storage and handling rules applied to a home hot tub: temperature, moisture, separation, labels, plus never-mix reminders.

CDC says pool chemicals can injure people when mixed together or when protective equipment isn’t used, and to store each one separately in its original labeled container below 95°F, out of the sun and protected from getting wet[15].

## Storage rules (CDC)

- Store below 95°F (35°C), in low humidity and out of direct sunlight, or as the manufacturer directs[15].

- Protect from getting wet[15].

- Store each chemical separately; keep incompatible chemicals away from each other; keep chemicals in original, manufacturer-labeled containers[15].

- Keep away from heat sources and flames; don’t store ignition sources such as gas-powered equipment with chemicals[15].

- Store and consume food and drinks away from pool chemicals[15].

- Limit access, especially to children and animals[15].

- Dispose of old, unwanted or unlabeled chemicals safely: contact the manufacturer or your local hazardous-materials group[15].

## Handling

- Read the label and keep the safety data sheet and protective equipment available[15].

- Never mix different chemicals together. Unicel specifically warns never to mix chlorine and acid[4].

- Add chemicals only through the filter compartment with jets on high as Hot Spring directs, taking care not to splash hands, eyes or shell[9].

- Water temperature: CPSC says 104°F or below[16].

## A practical kit (editorial)
A small bin that stays dry, a dedicated measuring scoop per product (never reused between chemicals), splash-resistant goggles and gloves, a good test kit and the product labels. See the product guides for sanitizer, shock and pH balance.
Product lists below are picks, not rankings. We checked that each Amazon listing exists and what its title says; we have not lab-tested any product, and we do not publish prices or star ratings because they change. Match any product to your spa maker’s guidance, and keep the label directions as your final word.

## Why do two spa filters the same size have different square-foot ratings?

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/why-same-size-spa-filters-have-different-square-feet/
Last updated: 2026-10-25

Same diameter, same length, but 25, 37 or 50 sq ft? Unicel’s 2026 spec table shows it is the pleat count, and what that means when you replace a cartridge.

The square-foot number is the total area of filter media folded into the cartridge, not its outside size. Two cartridges with the same diameter, length and end caps can hold different amounts of media because one has more pleats: in Unicel’s 2026 table, 106, 158 and 212 pleats in the same 4-15/16" × 13-5/16" body are rated 25, 37 and 50 sq ft[5]. So size alone cannot tell you the rating; the part number, or the pleat count, can.

## How the number is calculated

Unicel publishes its method for computing a cartridge’s area: count the pleats and measure the pleat height (the “amplitude”), measure the usable length of the media (excluding end caps and handles), then multiply the pleats by 2, by the pleat height, and by the usable length, and divide by 144. Its worked example is a cartridge with 75 pleats of 0.625" height and 9-1/4" of usable length: (75 × 2 × 0.625 × 9.25) ÷ 144 = 6.02 sq ft[5]. So area depends on three things: how many pleats, how tall each pleat is, and how long the media is. The outside diameter and overall length you can measure with a tape do not by themselves fix any of the three, which is how two cartridges that look identical can carry different amounts of media.

## The same-size pairs in Unicel’s spec table

Unicel’s 2026 Replacement Guide lists each cartridge’s outside diameter (OD), length, end-cap openings, pleat count, media weight and rated area[5]. Where several cartridges share the same OD, length and openings, the pleat count is what separates them. These are the groups in the table (Unicel’s own figures, quoted as printed from the 4000, 5000 and 6000 Series pages, printed pp. 5, 6 and 8; the area method is on p. 74):

OD × lengthUnicel P/NPleatsMediaRated areaListed for

4-15/16" × 13-5/16"
2-1/8" open both endsC-43261063 oz25 sq ftRainbow, Waterway Plastics, Custom Molded Products

C-46251064 oz25 sq ftsame brands as C-4326

C-46371584 oz37 sq ftRainbow, Waterway Plastics, Morgan Spas, Leisure Bay Spas, Custom Molded Products

C-49502123 oz50 sq ftRainbow, Waterway Plastics, Custom Molded Products

4-15/16" × 14-7/8"
2-1/8" open both endsC-43011063 oz28 sq ftMartec, Sonfarrel

C-43051933 oz50 sq ftCal Spas, Martec, Sonfarrel, Advantage Mfg.

5" × 13-5/16"
2-3/8" open both ends, no center coreC-56251034 oz25 sq ftJacuzzi CFR-25 (in-line)

C-56351584 oz37 sq ftJacuzzi CFR-37 (in-line)

5-3/16" × 12-1/2"
bar handle, 2" male thread5CH-3521513 oz35 sq ftMarquis Spas (new style)

5CH-5021973 oz50 sq ftMarquis Spas (new style), Cal Spas

6" × 8-1/4"
handle top, injection-molded 1-1/2" SAE thread6CH-9251323 oz25 sq fttop load

6CH-9402253 oz45 sq fttop load

6" × 14"
1-15/16" open both endsC-63501423 oz50 sq ftHot Springs Spas / Watkins (Limelight)

C-63552293 oz75 sq ftHot Springs Spas / Watkins (Limelight)

Within each group, more pleats means a larger rated area. (The table does not list pleat height, so we cannot show the full calculation for these rows.) In the first group, Unicel prints all four cartridges in one block of its table, and its guide says that cartridges listed between horizontal lines are interchangeable[5]. Two rows also show that media weight is a separate spec: C-4326 and C-4625 both have 106 pleats and 25 sq ft, but one uses 3 oz media and the other 4 oz[5]. Matching the square footage alone does not mean you are matching the cartridge.

## What Unicel says about the “upgrade” cartridges

Unicel’s maintenance page tells dealers to check its guide for an “upgraded surface area” cartridge when selling a replacement; as its example it names C-4637 as an upgrade for C-4625, with 12 more square feet and “all other dimensions the same”[4]. The guide marks the same relationship in its notes: C-4637 and C-4950 are listed as upgrades to the 25 sq ft C-4326 and C-4625[5]. Two Marquis replacements are described the same way: C-5423 (“the original was 25 sq. ft. (115 pleats). This replacement has been upgraded to 35 sq. ft.”) and C-5434 (original 40 sq ft, 109 pleats; upgraded to 60 sq ft)[5].

Unicel’s stated reason is flow per square foot: “cartridge filters can work at any flow rate. In fact, the lower the flow per square foot, the more efficient the system works”[4]. In a spa, where the pump moves a fixed amount of water, a cartridge with more media spreads that flow over more area. That is arithmetic from Unicel’s statement, not a test result we ran.

What we could not find: a spa manufacturer statement that says a higher-area cartridge of identical outside dimensions is approved, or not approved, for a particular spa. Unicel’s “upgrade” notes apply to cartridges whose other dimensions are the same, so check the end-cap openings and length as well as the area, and ask your spa dealer if your spa is under warranty.

## A real example where the sources disagree: Hot Spring Limelight (2018 and newer)

Unicel’s Hot Spring cross-reference ties both C-6350 (50 sq ft, 142 pleats) and C-6355 (75 sq ft, 229 pleats) to the Limelight cartridge, OEM 1642301-1 / 78161, and notes that the original is 6-3/8" OD while its replacements are 6"[5]. A Hot Spring dealer’s product page for 78161 gives 50 sq ft, 14" long, about 6-1/4" OD with open 2" ends[24]. Pleatco’s 2023 catalog lists the same OEM number as PWK35B at 6-3/8" × 14" and 35 sq ft[2]. That is three different ratings (75, 50 and 35 sq ft) for what the sources treat as one factory part.

We cannot tell from these documents which number is “right”, and we are not going to pick one. Dealer listings are not a reliable tie-breaker either: the same dealer’s pages list 260 pleats for both the Limelight 78161 (50 sq ft) and the Caldera 73531 (75 sq ft)[24][25], so we use pleat counts only from Unicel’s table. For a Limelight, order by the OEM number (78161 or 1642301-1) and compare the cartridge’s OD, length and end caps, rather than by the square-foot figure.

## How to tell which one you have

- Read the part number on the end cap or label. It beats every other method.

- If it has worn off, measure the OD, the length and the size of the top and bottom openings, and note whether the top has a handle or thread. Our how to find your spa filter size guide and the size lookup do this step.

- Count the pleats if two candidates share the same body: mark one fold with tape and count every fold around the circumference. Unicel’s own lookup instructions include counting the pleats (±2) and noting whether there is a center core[5], so a count within two of a listed number is a match.

- Use square footage last. Look at it only after the dimensions and end caps agree, and expect different catalogs to round it differently.

Once you know the cartridge, OEM vs Unicel vs Pleatco explains how the brands’ numbers line up.

## Hot tub flow error (FLO, FL1, HFL, LF, dr): is it the filter?

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/hot-tub-flow-error-codes-and-your-filter/
Last updated: 2026-10-26

What FLO, FL--1, HFL, LF, dr, HL and Hot Spring’s E2 No Flow mean, why a dirty filter is the first suspect, and the order to check things in, from Gecko, Balboa, Sundance, Hot Spring and Jacuzzi documents.

A flow error means the control system is not seeing enough water moving through the heater, so it turns the heater off to protect it. Every manufacturer document we checked lists a dirty or blocked filter among the first causes, along with low water, an air lock, closed valves or jets, and a pump that isn’t running or primed[26][27][12][29]. With the power off, check the water level, take the filter out and rinse or replace it, purge any air, then restore power and reset. If the error comes back with a clean filter and full water, Jacuzzi and Sundance say to call a dealer or technician[10][12].

## What each code means

The code depends on who made your spa’s control system, not on the filter brand. These are the flow-related messages in the documents we checked:

Code on the panelControl / brandWhat the manufacturer says it meansReset, per the document

FLOGecko (in.ye, in.yt, in.yj, in.xe)No water flow detected while the main pump runs[26]Not stated; fix the cause first

HLGeckoWater in the heater reached 119 °F (48 °C) and the system stopped; Gecko says to make sure nothing is blocking flow, such as closed valves or a dirty or clogged filter[26]Turn the spa off and on

HFL (M016)BalboaHeater flow is reduced; the heater tries again after about 1 minute[27]Yes, it retries

LF (M017)BalboaNot enough flow, heater disabled. Balboa’s fault sheet says LF follows HFL occurring 5 times in 24 hours[27][28]Press any button after fixing

dr (M028)BalboaHeater may be dry; spa shuts down for 15 minutes[27]Press any button to reset

dry / dY (M027)BalboaHeater is dry and the spa is shut down; the fault sheet says this follows dr 3 times in a row[27][28]Press any button after fixing

OHH (M030)Balboa118 °F (47.8 °C) detected in the heater; spa shut down[27]Press a button once water is below 108 °F

FL--1 “FLOW ERROR OPEN”Sundance 780 SeriesFlow switch open: the switch is faulty, the filter is excessively dirty, or there is an air lock at the circulation pump intake. The heater turns off and jets pump 1 may too[12]Not stated; dealer if it persists

FL--2 “FLOW ERROR CLOSED”Sundance 780 SeriesFlow switch stuck closed[12]Not stated; contact the dealer

FL--3 “FLOW ERROR TOGGLE”Sundance 780 SeriesFlow switch behaving erratically; Sundance says clean the filters and correct the water level before calling the dealer[12]Not stated

E2: NO FLOW-CHECK FILTER, yellow status lightHot Spring Highlife (2023)No-flow / pressure-switch fault; heater off. Hot Spring says check and clean the filter, then call for service if needed[29]The pressure switch closes once flow is restored[29]

Jacuzzi’s filter page describes FLO and low-flow messages the same way: the system isn’t detecting enough circulation[10].

## Check these in order

- Turn the power off before you open the filter compartment. Jacuzzi says this stops the pump starting unexpectedly and avoids drawing air into the plumbing[10].

- Check the water level. Sundance’s fix for FL--1 and FL--2 starts with water above all the jets but below the lowest pillow[12]. Balboa’s flow checks start with low water too[27].

- Take the filter out, rinse it and look at it. Sundance, Gecko, Hot Spring and Jacuzzi all name a dirty or clogged filter[12][26][29][10]. Jacuzzi says to inspect for damage while you rinse[10]. If it is torn, crushed or no longer recovers with cleaning, see signs your filter is bad.

- Purge any air lock. Sundance’s method: with the filter out, hold a garden hose over the filter wall fitting with a rag sealing around the hose end, run the water for 30 seconds, then reinstall the filter[12]. Gecko’s method: with the pump running, slowly loosen one pump union nut to let trapped air out, then retighten it[26].

- Open valves and jets. Gecko and Balboa list closed valves; Balboa adds too many closed jets[26][27].

- Make sure the pump that feeds the heater is running. Gecko says to confirm the main pump runs; Sundance says to cycle power at the breaker if the circulation pump isn’t running[26][12].

- Reset. Balboa LF, dr and dry need a button press after the fix[27]. Some errors need the power removed and restored[27].

## Got the error right after cleaning or refilling?

That is a common pattern, and the documents point to air or water level rather than the clean filter. Hot Spring lists draining the spa without disconnecting power, and air locks in the plumbing, as causes of pressure-switch and thermal cut-off trips[29]. Sundance says that if filling through the footwell gives you an air lock, fill through the filter inlet instead[12]. On Balboa systems the spa enters Priming Mode at every power-up for 4 minutes so you can check each pump is primed, and the heater cannot run in that mode[27]. Jacuzzi also lists recurring FLO errors right after cleaning as one of the signs a cartridge needs replacing rather than cleaning[10].

## Can I run the spa without the filter to see if the error clears?

The manufacturers we checked don’t recommend it. Sundance has you take the filter out only to purge air, and to reinstall it before turning the power back on[12]. Jacuzzi advises against running the spa with no filter installed, because unfiltered water carries contaminants to the pumps and heater, and suggests keeping a second clean cartridge to swap in[10].

## When it isn’t the filter

- Sundance FL--2 is a flow switch stuck closed, which a clean filter won’t fix[12].

- Gecko FLO that persists: Gecko’s checklist also asks for a minimum flow of 68 L/min (18 US gal/min) and a properly plugged-in in.flo cable above the heater; if FLO still persists, it says to replace the heater and then the control system[26]. Those steps are for a technician.

- Hot Spring: call for service if the heater trips frequently[29].

- Any brand: if the spa won’t circulate or heat with a new, clean filter and balanced water, Jacuzzi says it needs professional diagnosis, and that running a faulty system can damage other parts[10].

## Preventing it

A filter that is cleaned on schedule is less likely to restrict flow; see how often to clean a hot tub filter and how to clean one. If you need a replacement, search by part number, or use the model-year lookups for Hot Spring, Caldera, Jacuzzi, Sundance, Bullfrog and Master Spas.

- Balboa Water Group — TP600 and TP400 User Guide (heater-related messages and flow-related checks): https://www.balboawater.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/TP600-and-TP400-USER-GUIDE_Standard-Menus_40940.pdf

## Open-end vs threaded hot tub filters: how to tell which fitting you have

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/open-end-vs-threaded-hot-tub-filters/
Last updated: 2026-10-27

Why two spa cartridges with the same diameter and length can still be the wrong filter: open ends, handles, male slip, MPT and SAE threads, from the Unicel and Pleatco spec fields.

Match the top and the bottom, not just the outside size. Unicel’s and Pleatco’s spec tables print an opening size, a handle, a male slip or a thread for each end[5][2]. A 7" × 10-3/4" Caldera cartridge with a 2" male slip bottom (C-7451, OEM 033016) is not the same fitting as the 7" × 10-3/4" cartridge with a 2-11/16" open bottom (C-7350, OEM 1019401), even though both are listed at 50 sq ft with a handle on top.

## What the catalogs actually list

A spa filter cartridge is a stack of pleated media between two end caps. The outside diameter and the overall length tell you whether the cartridge fits the well. The end caps tell you whether it seals. Unicel’s 2026 Replacement Guide and the Pleatco 2023 catalog both give those four fields for each cartridge: diameter, length, top and bottom[5][2]. Square footage is a fifth field, and it describes media area, not the shape of the cap. Our square-foot guide covers that difference. This page is about the caps.

When you pull the old cartridge, look at each end before you measure across the pleats. The patterns that show up over and over in the spec tables are:

- Open both ends. A round hole in the top cap and a round hole in the bottom cap. The catalog prints the hole size, for example 1-15/16" or 2-1/8". The cartridge slides over a standpipe or sits between two sealing surfaces in the housing.

- Handle on top, thread on the bottom. The top is a molded cone, a bar, or a semi-circular handle you grab to pull the cartridge out. The bottom is a male thread, printed as MPT or as an SAE thread of a stated size.

- Handle on top, male slip on the bottom. The bottom is a smooth pipe-like stub, not a thread. Caldera’s older 7" cartridges are printed this way.

- Handle on top, open bottom. Common on later Caldera cartridges: you still lift it by a handle, but the bottom is an open hole with a stated inside diameter instead of a slip fitting.

- Closed or castle top. Some Sundance cartridges are printed with a castle top or a closed top and an open bottom of a specific size. The top is not a hole you can see through.

None of those descriptions is a guess about how a spa “usually” works. Each one is a column in the spec table for a particular part number[5][2].

## Same length, different bottom: Caldera’s 7" cartridges

Caldera’s Paradise, Utopia and Highland collections use several 7"-diameter cartridges with a semi-circular handle. Two lengths show up: 10-3/4" and 14-3/4". Inside each length, the bottom changed.

UnicelOEMSizeBottom, as printedPleatcoArea

C-74510330167" × 10-3/4"2" male slipPCD5050 sq ft

C-73501019401; 735327" × 10-3/4"2-11/16" openPCD50N50 sq ft

C-74790330177" × 14-3/4"2" male slipPCD7575 sq ft

C-73751019301; 735317" × 14-3/4"2-11/16" openPCD75N75 sq ft

A tape measure across the pleats will not separate C-7451 from C-7350. You have to look at the bottom. The Unicel note on the C-7451 row says C-7350 can also be used, and the note on C-7479 says C-7375 can also be used[5]. That is an interchange note from Unicel, not a statement that the bottoms are printed the same. If your old cartridge still has a 2" male slip stub, order the slip-bottom number and compare it with the cartridge in your hand. If the bottom is an open hole, order the open-bottom number. The longer pair is the same story at 14-3/4". Read Caldera filter bottoms before you buy for a Paradise, Utopia or Highland tub, and use the Caldera model-year lookup when you know the model.

## Open both ends: the Hot Spring footprint

Many Hot Spring cartridges have no thread at all. C-6430 is 6" in diameter and 10-1/2" long, open 1-15/16" at both ends, rated 30 sq ft. Unicel, Pleatco and Filbur list it for OEM 31489 (also printed as 71825 and 71826), as Pleatco PWK30-4 and Filbur FC-3915[5][2][31]. C-8465 is the larger open cartridge: 8-1/2" × 10-1/2", open 3" at both ends, 65 sq ft, OEM 31114 / 71827 / 71828, Pleatco PWK65, Filbur FC-3960[5][2][31]. Both are open-end filters. They are not interchangeable with each other, because the diameter and the hole size differ. A full walk-through of which collection uses which one is in Hot Spring filter sizes by collection.

Open-end cartridges in the 4-15/16" family are just as specific. C-4335 is 4-15/16" × 9-1/4" with 2-1/8" open ends (OEM 74148, Pleatco PRB35-IN, 35 sq ft). C-4326 is 4-15/16" × 13-5/16" with the same 2-1/8" open ends, at 25 sq ft. The hole size matches. The length does not. Ordering by diameter alone would mix them.

## Threads: MPT and SAE are both “threaded,” and they are not one size

Where the catalog says “male thread” or “MPT,” the bottom screws onto a fitting. Where it says “SAE thread,” it also screws on, but the thread series is the SAE thread printed for that part, not a generic pipe thread. The spec table gives the size either way[5].

- Sundance 4CH-35, OEM 6540-486, is 4-5/8" × 16" with a molded cone handle and a 1-1/2" male MPT bottom, 40 sq ft.

- Bullfrog 8CH-951, OEM 10-2870, is an 8" cartridge 5-3/4" long with a semi-circular handle and a 2" SAE thread. Pleatco lists it as PBF36[2].

- Jacuzzi 6CH-960 is 6-3/4" × 15-1/2" with a semi-circular handle and a 2" SAE thread. The look-alike 6CH-961 uses the same OEM numbers in Unicel’s table but is printed “open with slots” on top, and Unicel says it requires an injection-molded semi-circular handle that is not furnished[5].

A 1-1/2" MPT bottom will not become a 2" SAE bottom because the lengths are close. If the old cartridge’s thread is worn, match the OEM number molded into the cap before you match the thread you can still see. Sundance and Jacuzzi look-alike filters goes through the pairs that share a body and not a fitting.

## How to check the fitting on the cartridge in your hand

- Turn the spa off before you open the filter well. Hot Spring and Jacuzzi both say to cut power first[9][10].

- Read any number on the end cap or the band. Search it from the homepage. A readable OEM, Unicel or Pleatco number beats a measurement.

- If the number is gone, measure the outside diameter across the pleats and the overall length, including a handle or a threaded nipple. Then write down the top and the bottom in words: open (and the hole size, if you can measure the inside), handle, closed, slip, or thread. The measuring guide and the size lookup use the same fields the catalogs use.

- Compare your notes with the top and bottom lines on the cartridge page, not only with the diameter and length.

- If two pages share a size, open both. The one whose ends match is the one to order.

Pleatco’s cleaning sheet makes a related point about the media itself: a cartridge can look stained and still be the right part, and a white cartridge is not automatically a clean one[3]. Stain is not a fitting. The end cap is.

## What to do when the sources disagree about the hole

They sometimes do. On the Intex Type S1 cartridge, Unicel prints 2-1/16" open ends and Pleatco prints 1-5/8", while both print the body as 4-1/4" × 2-15/16"[5][2]. Our Intex C-4317 page keeps both figures and tells you the body size is the part they agree on. When a page on this site says the catalogs disagree, order by the manufacturer’s part number and hold the new cartridge next to the old one before you drop it in the well.

Replacement intervals and cleaning are separate decisions. A correct fitting does not tell you how old the media is. Use how often to replace a hot tub filter and signs the filter is bad for that, and how to install a cartridge once the part number matches.

## Hot Spring filter sizes by collection: Highlife, Limelight and Tiger River

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/hot-spring-filter-sizes-by-collection/
Last updated: 2026-10-27

Which Hot Spring cartridge is the 6" open filter, which is the 8-1/2" open filter, and which Limelight part the catalogs rate three different ways. OEM numbers 31489, 71825, 71827 and 78161.

Most Highlife spas in our cited listings use the 6" × 10-1/2" open cartridge C-6430 (OEM 31489 / 71825 / 71826, 30 sq ft). Many 2008–2017 Limelight and Tiger River models in those listings use the 8-1/2" × 10-1/2" open cartridge C-8465 (OEM 31114 / 71827 / 71828, 65 sq ft). 2018-and-later Limelight models in the same listings use OEM 78161 / 1642301-1, which Unicel lists as both a 50 sq ft and a 75 sq ft 6" × 14" cartridge[5][38][39][24].

## Three bodies, not one “Hot Spring filter”

Hot Spring is built by Watkins, and the brand has reused a small set of cartridge sizes across many collections. That reuse is why a model name alone is a weak way to order. The end cap number is the strong way. The three bodies below are the ones the Unicel 2026 guide, the Pleatco 2023 catalog, the Filbur catalog and the Leisure Time Inc. listings agree enough to publish. Where they do not agree, the paragraph says so.

Collection, from the cited listingOEM numbersUnicelSize and endsArea on our row

Highlife models named for 71825, many from 1990 onward31489; 71825; 71826C-64306" × 10-1/2", open 1-15/16" both ends30 sq ft

Limelight 2008–2017 and Tiger River models named for 7182731114; 71827; 71828C-84658-1/2" × 10-1/2", open 3" both ends65 sq ft

Limelight 2018–2026 models named for 781611642301-1; 78161C-6350 and C-63556" × 14", open 1-15/16" both ends. Unicel notes the original OD is 6-3/8"50 sq ft (C-6350) and 75 sq ft (C-6355)

Pleatco’s cross-reference lists C-6430 as PWK30-4 and C-8465 as PWK65[2]. Filbur lists FC-3915 and FC-3960 for those same OEM numbers[31]. The 2018 Limelight cartridge is the one the catalogs do not line up, and it has its own section below. Model-by-model years are on the Hot Spring filter by model and year page and on each cartridge page.

## The 6" Highlife cartridge, and the Tri-X warning

C-6430 is an open-end cartridge: no handle threads onto the housing. Unicel dates the Hot Spring use of this size to models after 1990 and prints the media as 4 oz[5]. The Leisure Time listing for OEM 71825 says many of these hot tubs take three cartridges at once, and that some models use a Tri-X ceramic filter of the same footprint instead of a pleated cartridge. The same listing says to use the pleated cartridge only where the spa specifies 71825 or a listed equivalent, and that a model which requires Tri-X needs the Tri-X filter[38].

That is a practical check, not a slogan. If you open the well and find a ceramic block rather than pleated fabric, C-6430 is the wrong object even if the footprint matches. If you find three pleated cartridges, order three. Hot Spring’s own maintenance page tells owners to replace with genuine Watkins filters[7]. An aftermarket cross-reference matches size and fittings; it is not a Watkins part. Warranty language is in your owner’s manual, not in a catalog table.

Hot Spot and some Solana models are assigned this same 6" × 10-1/2" cartridge by the dealer listings we cite, which is why those brands point back at the Hot Spring tables. Start at Hot Spot or Solana if that is the badge on the cabinet, then confirm the end-cap number.

## The 8-1/2" cartridge for earlier Limelight and Tiger River

C-8465 is larger in diameter (8-1/2") and shorter than the 2018 Limelight cartridge. Both ends are open 3". Unicel, Pleatco and Filbur agree on OEM 31114 / 71827 / 71828, Pleatco PWK65 and Filbur FC-3960, at 65 sq ft[5][2][31]. The Leisure Time listing for 71827 is the source of the model years on that page: Limelight Bolt 2012–2017, Flair, Glow and Pulse 2008–2017, and a long Tiger River list that includes Bengal, Caspian, Sumatran and others going back to the early 1990s[39].

Do not put this cartridge in a 2018-or-later Limelight that calls for 78161. The diameter is 8-1/2", not 6", and the length is 10-1/2", not 14". The open-end vs threaded guide shows why the hole size matters even when you have already matched the brand.

## 2018 and newer Limelight: one OEM number, three area ratings

Unicel’s Hot Spring cross-reference ties both C-6350 (50 sq ft, 142 pleats) and C-6355 (75 sq ft, 229 pleats) to OEM 1642301-1 / 78161. Both replacements are printed 6" × 14" with 1-15/16" open ends, and Unicel notes that the original cartridge is 6-3/8" OD while the replacements are 6"[5]. A Leisure Time product page for 78161 gives 50 sq ft, 14" long, and about 6-1/4" OD with open 2" ends[24]. Pleatco’s 2023 catalog lists the same OEM number as PWK35B at 6-3/8" × 14" and 35 sq ft[2]. Those are three different area ratings — 75, 50 and 35 sq ft — for what the sources treat as one factory part.

We do not pick a winner. Our C-6350 page leaves the Pleatco equivalent off because PWK35B’s printed size and area do not match Unicel’s 6" / 50 sq ft row. The C-6355 page shows PWK35B and repeats the disagreement. For a 2018-or-later Limelight Beam, Flair, Flash or Pulse, order by 78161 or 1642301-1 and compare OD, length and the open ends with the old cartridge. The dealer listing we cite names those five Limelight models for 2018–2026[24].

The arithmetic Unicel publishes for area is pleats × 2 × pleat height × usable length ÷ 144[5]. That is why two cartridges with the same outside size can carry different ratings. It is also why a rating, by itself, is the wrong thing to shop for. The worked examples live in why same-size filters have different square-foot ratings.

## Other Hot Spring numbers that are easy to mix in

Not every Hot Spring row is one of the three bodies above. 4CH-35 is OEM 31382 (formerly 31116): 4-5/8" × 16", molded cone handle, 1-1/2" male MPT, 35 sq ft, Pleatco PTL35-4, Filbur FC-0161. No model-year list is in the sources for that row, so we do not invent one. C-6330 shares the 6" × 10-1/2" open body and the 30 sq ft rating with C-6430 but is listed under OEM 31489 as its own Unicel number; read that page before assuming the two Unicel numbers are identical in every column. C-6600 is a different body again: 6-3/8" × 11-7/8", open 3" both ends.

If the number on your cap is not in this article, search it. The cross-reference is the index. This article is the map of the three sizes people confuse.

## Care, once the size is right

Hot Spring’s filter article says a standard polyester cartridge is typically replaced every 2–3 years, and a TRI-X cartridge every 4–6 years[8]. The owner maintenance page says every three years[7]. Those are different sentences from the same brand, so treat them as a range and replace sooner if the media is torn or flow does not come back after a clean. The Hot Spot collection manual says to turn power off before removing filters, not to run the spa with the cartridge removed, and not to overtighten the retainer[9]. Cleaning steps are in how to clean a hot tub filter. A clogged cartridge is also the first thing Hot Spring names when a spa shows a no-flow fault; see what a clogged or missing filter does.

## Caldera filter bottoms: male slip, open end, and the 2014 Cantabria split

URL: https://myspafilter.com/guides/caldera-filter-bottom-fittings/
Last updated: 2026-10-27

Caldera 7" and 8" cartridges that share a length and not a bottom fitting, including OEM 033016 vs 1019401 and the 74817 / 73722 quarter split on Utopia Cantabria.

On Caldera’s 7" handle cartridges, the older parts have a 2" male slip bottom (C-7451, OEM 033016, and C-7479, OEM 033017) and the later parts have a 2-11/16" open bottom (C-7350, OEM 1019401, and C-7375, OEM 1019301 / 73531)[5]. On the 8" × 16-1/2" pair, Leisure Time says Utopia Cantabria uses OEM 74817 through the second quarter of 2014 and OEM 73722 from the third quarter of 2014 on[41][40]. Look at the bottom of the old cartridge either way.

## Why Caldera has two filters that measure the same

Caldera and Hot Spring come from the same Watkins factory, but most Caldera collections do not use the Hot Spring open-end cartridge. Paradise, Utopia and Highland models in the cited listings use a 7"-diameter cartridge with a semi-circular handle on top. The length is either 10-3/4" (about 50 sq ft in the rows below) or 14-3/4" (about 75 sq ft). The detail that changed over time is the bottom.

UnicelOEMPleatcoFilburSizeBottom

C-7451033016PCD50FC-30847" × 10-3/4"2" male slip

C-73501019401; 73532PCD50NFC-39637" × 10-3/4"2-11/16" open

C-7479033017PCD75FC-30857" × 14-3/4"2" male slip

C-73751019301; 73531PCD75NFC-39647" × 14-3/4"2-11/16" open

Unicel’s note on C-7451 says C-7350 can also be used, and the note on C-7479 says C-7375 can also be used[5]. Read that as Unicel’s interchange note, and still look at the cartridge you removed. A male slip is a stub that pushes into a fitting. An open bottom is a hole. If you still have the stub, the slip-bottom part is the one the spec row describes. If you have a hole about 2-11/16" across, the open-bottom part is the one the spec row describes. Pleatco marks the open-bottom numbers with an N (PCD50N, PCD75N) and the slip-bottom numbers without it (PCD50, PCD75)[2].

The open-bottom 14-3/4" cartridge is the one with the long model list. C-7375 is cited for Utopia Geneva, Hawaiian, Niagara, Provence and Tahitian years, and for Paradise Geneva, Hawaiian, Makena, Moorea, Niagara, Reunion, Salina and Seychelles years, among others. Two of those lines carry an extra warning from Leisure Time: a 2004 Hawaiian HAA and a 2024 Makena need a serial-number check before you order[5]. The short open-bottom cartridge, C-7350, is the one cited for later Utopia Ravello, several Paradise models including a 2024-only Makena note, and Highland Cascade, Cumberland, San Gabriel and Teton. The Caldera model-year lookup is the index of those rows. A model name without the year is how people order the slip bottom for a spa that left the factory with the open bottom.

## The 8" Cantabria cartridges are a quarter-year problem

Two Caldera cartridges share an 8" diameter, a 16-1/2" length and a 100 sq ft rating, and they do not share end caps.

- C-8300, OEM 74817, Filbur FC-3966. Top and bottom are 3-1/8" open with a molded gasket. No Pleatco number is shown: the Leisure Time listing also names Pleatco PWK100, and PWK100 is not in the Pleatco 2023 spec tables, so we do not list it as an equivalent. The cited fitment is Utopia Cantabria 2009 through the second quarter of 2014. Leisure Time says to confirm the production quarter on a 2014 Cantabria, because third and fourth quarter production uses 73722[41].

- C-8399, OEM 1039607 / 73722, Pleatco PCD100W, Filbur FC-3965. The top is a semi-circular handle and the bottom is 3-5/8" open with a lip seal. Leisure Time says this is the cartridge for Cantabria from the third quarter of 2014 onward, and that first and second quarter 2014 uses 74817[40]. The same listing names later Utopia Geneva, Niagara, Tahitian, Florence and Elation years, plus Aquatic Melodies Aspire and Elation for 2005–2008.

A 2014 Cantabria owner who only knows the model name has a coin flip. The serial number or the production quarter is the tie-break, and the cartridge in the spa is the better one. Measure the bottom: a 3-1/8" opening with gaskets is the C-8300 description; a handle and a 3-5/8" lip-seal bottom is the C-8399 description.

## Vacanza is the Caldera line that borrows Hot Spring sizes

Vacanza Marino, Palatino (2010–2026) and Vanto (2011–2026) are listed on Caldera C-8465 for OEM 76136: 8-1/2" × 10-1/2", open 3" both ends, 65 sq ft, Pleatco PWK65, Filbur FC-3960. That is the same Unicel body as Hot Spring’s 71827 cartridge, with a Caldera OEM number. Caldera C-6430 is the 6" × 10-1/2" open cartridge under OEM 31489, shared with Hot Spring Highlife. If your Caldera is a Vacanza, do not assume it takes the 7" handle cartridge the Paradise and Utopia listings use. Read the end cap, or start at the model-year table.

C-4335 (OEM 74148, Pleatco PRB35-IN) and C-4950 (OEM 302005, Pleatco PRB50-IN) are the smaller open-end Caldera cartridges, 4-15/16" in diameter, 9-1/4" and 13-5/16" long. They are a third family. The fitting guide open-end vs threaded puts the three families side by side.

## How to order without guessing the year

- Read the OEM number on the cartridge. 033016 and 033017 are the slip-bottom pair. 1019401, 73532, 1019301 and 73531 are the open-bottom pair. 74817 and 73722 are the 8" pair.

- If the number is gone, measure diameter, length, and the bottom. Write “slip,” “open,” or “gasket,” and the size of the opening if you can take it.

- For a 2014 Cantabria, get the production quarter or compare the ends with the two descriptions above[40][41].

- For a 2024 Makena or a 2004 Hawaiian, the cited listing says to check the serial number[5].

- Then confirm on the cartridge page, which cites the catalog page the numbers came from. How Filbur, Unicel and Pleatco numbers compare shows what those three columns mean.

Hot Spring’s chemical page is the one we cite for Watkins water ranges if you are balancing after a filter change: free chlorine 1–5 ppm, pH 7.2–7.8, alkalinity 40–120 ppm, calcium hardness 75–150 ppm on a standard system[18]. The filter fitting and the water chemistry are different jobs. A correct bottom does not fix a low sanitizer reading, and a bottle of balancer does not seal a slip fitting.
